After two years Porcius Festus came into his place, and Felix left Paulos bound to do a favor to the Yehudaye (Acts 24:27).

Paulos said he was brought up "at the side of the feet of Gamaliel" and instructed perfectly in the law of the fathers (Acts 22:3).

names.note: Hebrews 7:1 says, "this Melkizedeq is king of Shalem, priest of Elohim the Most High," and that he met Avraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him. Hebrews 7:2 explains that king of Shalem is "king of peace."

The Peshitta writes this place ܫܠܝܡ. This book prints Shalim. The familiar English is Salim, the town near Ein-Yon where Yochanan was immersing. The same letters name Shalem, the city of Melkizedeq, in Hebrews.

root.source: Strong’s G4539 Σαλώμη: “probably of Hebrew origin (feminine from H7965)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: One of the women at the cross and the tomb, Mark 15:40 and 16:1. The familiar English is Salome. The same letters are also the ordinary word for peace. This book does not give her a father's name.

sources.note: The Greek writing of this woman in Mark.

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܫܡܪܝܬܐ. This book prints Shamraye. The familiar English is Samaritan woman. Read from the Syriac letters: shamrayta.

root.source: Strong’s G4540 Σαμάρεια: “of Hebrew origin (H8111)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Samaria.
The Greek writing.

names.note: The wife of Chananya in Acts 5. The familiar English is Sapphira. The same letters are also the ordinary word for good.

sources.note: The Greek writing of her name.

root.source: Strong’s G4549 Σαούλ: “of Hebrew origin (H7586)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܫܐܘܠ. This book prints Shaul. The familiar English is Saul. Read from the Syriac letters: Shaul.

sources.note: The Hebrew writing. The Greek form of this man’s Hebrew name is Σαῦλος. Paulos is the other name.

root.source: Strong’s G4966 Συχέμ: “of Hebrew origin (H7927)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The place where Estephanos says the fathers were laid, in the tomb Avraham bought from the sons of Hamor, Acts 7:16. The familiar English is Shechem. This is a city, not a man.

sources.note: The Hebrew name of the city.
The Greek writing in Acts 7:16.

root.source: Strong’s G4528 Σαλαθιήλ: “of Hebrew origin (H7597)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܫܠܬܐܝܠ. This book prints Shelatiel. The familiar English is Shealtiel. Read from the Syriac letters: shaltayel.

sources.note: I asked of God. The Greek writes Σαλαθιήλ.

names.note: The place of the dead. Murdock renders the gates of Sheol as “the gates of death.”

sources.note: The Hebrew name of the place of the dead. The Greek often writes ᾅδης for the same place.

root.source: Strong’s G4609 Σίλας: “contraction for G4610 (Σιλουανός)”; Strong’s G4610 Σιλουανός: “of Latin origin” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: One of the leading men among the brothers and a prophet, sent from Urishlim to Antiokia with Paulos and Bar-Naba (Acts 15:22, 15:32). Paulos chose Shila as his companion (Acts 15:40). At Philippi the two were seized and dragged to the marketplace, scourged and thrown into the prison (Acts 16:12, 16:19, 16:23–24), and in the middle of the night they were praying and glorifying Elohim (Acts 16:25).

root.source: Strong’s G4611 Σιλωάμ: “of Hebrew origin (H7975)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Y'shua spoke of the eighteen on whom the tower in Shiloach fell and killed them, asking whether they were sinners more than all who live in Urishlim (Luke 13:2, 13:4). He made clay, spread it on the eyes of a man blind from his mother's womb and said, "Go wash in the immersion-pool of Shiloach," and the man washed and came seeing (John 9:1, 9:6–7). The man told it: "Go wash in the waters of Shiloach. And I went, washed, and I saw" (John 9:11).

root.source: Strong’s G4590 Σήμ: “of Hebrew origin (H8035)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܫܝܡ. This book prints Shim. The familiar English is Shem. Read from the Syriac letters: shim.

root.source: Strong’s G4613 Σίμων: “of Hebrew origin (H8095)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: One spelling, and this book itself separates the men. Shimon who is called Keefa. Shimon the Zealot, called the Qananya in the lists of the twelve. Shimon the tanner at Yoppa. Shimon the Qurinya, who carried the cross. Shimon the leper at Beth-Anya. Shimon who is called Niger, at Antiokia. And the Shimon in Shamrin who believed Philipos and then asked to buy the gift. The book also spells this name ܣܝܡܘܢ.

sources.note: The Hebrew writing. A few verses in this Peshitta use the Greek-shaped spelling ܣܝܡܘܢ instead.

root.source: Strong’s G4546 Σαμψών: “of Hebrew origin (H8123)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܫܡܫܘܢ. This book prints Shimshon. The familiar English is Samson. Read from the Syriac letters: shamshun.

root.source: Strong’s G4589 Σήθ: “of Hebrew origin (H8352)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܫܝܬ. This book prints Shith. The familiar English is Seth. Read from the Syriac letters: shith.

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Seth.

root.source: Strong’s G4965 Συχάρ: “of Hebrew origin (H7941)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this place ܫܟܪ. This book prints Shkar. The familiar English is Sychar. Read from the Syriac letters: shkar.

root.source: Strong’s G4672 Σολομών: “of Hebrew origin (H8010)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Son of Dawid by the wife of Uriya, in Matthew's genealogy (Matthew 1:6–7). Y'shua said that not even Shlemun in all his glory was clothed like the lilies, and that one greater than Shlemun is here (Matthew 6:29; 12:42). Shlemun built a house for the Elohim of Ya'akov (Acts 7:46–47), and a porch in the temple was called by his name (John 10:23; Acts 3:11).

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Solomon. The Greek is Σολομών.

root.source: Strong’s G4545 Σαμουήλ: “of Hebrew origin (H8050)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Shimon told the people that all the prophets from Shmuel and those after him proclaimed these days (Acts 3:12, 3:24). In the synagogue at Antiokia of Pisidia, Paulos said Elohim gave judges for four hundred and fifty years, "until Shmuel the prophet" (Acts 13:14, 13:16, 13:20). Hebrews 11:32 names Shmuel with Dawid and the rest of the prophets among those the writer has no time to tell of.

root.source: Strong’s G4677 Σουσάννα: “of Hebrew origin (H7799 feminine)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: One of the women who served Y'shua from their own possessions, Luke 8:3, with Yochan the wife of Kuza. The familiar English is Susanna. The same letters are also the word for a lily.

sources.note: The Greek writing. The Hebrew lily is שׁוֹשַׁן.

root.source: Strong’s G4610 Σιλουανός: “of Latin origin” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Paulos names Silwanus with himself and Timotheos as those by whom the Son of Elohim was preached to the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 1:1, 1:19). Paulos, Silwanus and Timotheos open both letters to the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Keefa writes, "I have written to you by Silwanus, a faithful brother" (1 Peter 5:12).

The messenger of Master YHWH appeared to Moshe in a fire burning in a bush in the wilderness of mount Sinai (Acts 7:29–30), and there Moshe received living words to give to us (Acts 7:37–38). Paulos writes that the covenant from mount Sinai, which gives birth to bondage, is Hagar, "the mountain Sinai that is in Arabia" (Galatians 4:24–25).

sources.note: The Hebrew writing. The Greek is Σινᾶ.

root.source: Strong’s G2469 Ἰσκαριώτης: “of Hebrew origin (probably H377 and H7149)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The surname of Yehuda, one of the twelve, who handed Y'shua over (Matthew 10:4; Luke 6:16); John calls him Yehuda son of Shimon Skaryota (John 6:71; 13:26). Satana entered into him, and he went to the chief priests to hand Y'shua over (Luke 22:3–4; Mark 14:10). John 14:22 marks another disciple as "Yehuda, not Sakaryuta."

root.source: Strong’s G4667 Σμύρνα: “the same as G4666 (σμύρνα)”; Strong’s G4666 σμύρνα: “apparently strengthened for G3464 (μύρον)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The later Syriac text writes this place ܙܡܘܪܢܐ. This book prints Smyrna. Read from the Syriac letters: Zmurna.

On the day Lut went out from Sdom, fire and brimstone rained from heaven and destroyed them all (Luke 17:29); 2 Peter 2:6 says Sodom and Amorah were burned and set as a demonstration to the wicked. Y'shua said it would be more comfortable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for a city that would not receive his disciples, or for Kfar-Nachum (Matthew 10:14–15; 11:23–24).

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Sodom. The Greek is Σόδομα.

names.note: Sopatrus of the city Berua, who went with Paulos as far as Asia, Acts 20:4. Romans 16:21 greets Sosipatros, written ܣܘܣܝܦܛܪܘܣ. The familiar English of both is Sosipater. The book does not say they are one man.

root.source: Strong’s G4988 Σωσθένης: “from the base of G4982 (σώζω) and that of G4599 (σθενόω)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܣܘܣܬܢܣ. This book prints Sosthenes. Read from the Syriac letters: Sostenes.

sources.note: A Greek name. The Syriac writes those sounds.

root.source: No dictionary source names the origin language (Strong’s G4681 Σπανία: “probably of foreign origin”); the label follows the Syriac verse form.

names.note: Paulos writes, "when I go to Spain, I hope to come and see you" (Romans 15:24). First he is going to Urishlim to serve the holy ones with the contribution from Macedonia and Achaia, and then, "I will pass by you to Spain" (Romans 15:25–26, 15:28).

root.source: Strong’s G4734 Στεφανᾶς: “probably contraction for … (crowned; from G4737 (στεφανόω))” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Paulos writes, "I immersed also the household of Stephanas" (1 Corinthians 1:1, 1:16). He calls that household the first-fruits of Achaia, who have set their soul to the service of the holy ones (1 Corinthians 16:15). He rejoiced at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, "for they have filled what you lacked toward me" (1 Corinthians 16:17).

sources.note: A Greek name, from stephanos, a wreath.

root.source: Follows the Syriac verse form (owner decision W-146). Strong’s H5488 סוּף: “probably of Egyptian origin” (Strong’s Dictionaries, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Estepanos said that Moshe brought the people out, doing signs and wonders in the land of Mitsrayin, in the Sea of Suf and in the wilderness forty years (Acts 6:15; 7:1, 7:35–36). Hebrews 11:29 says, "By faith they crossed the sea of Suf as on dry land," and in it "the Mitsraye were swallowed when they dared to enter it."
The Peshitta writes this person ܣܘܢܛܝܟܐ. This book prints Syntyche. Read from the Syriac letters: Syntyche.

The fame of Y'shua was heard in all Syria (Matthew 4:24), and Luke 2:2 dates the first enrollment to the governorship of Quirinius in Syria. The apostles and elders wrote to the brothers in Antiokia, Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:23), and Paulos traveled through Syria and Qiliqiya strengthening the assemblies (Acts 15:41).

sources.note: The Greek name of the land. This book also prints Syria.

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܛܒܝܬܐ. This book prints Tabitha. Read from the Syriac letters: tabita.

The Peshitta writes this person ܬܕܝ. This book prints Tadai. The familiar English is Thaddeus. Read from the Syriac letters: taday. In Matthew 10:3 the Peshitta calls him ܠܒܝ Lebbai (lebbay), surnamed Tadai; the familiar English is Lebbaeus, called Thaddeus.

root.source: Strong’s G2283 Θάμαρ: “of Hebrew origin (H8559)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܬܡܪ. This book prints Tamar. Read from the Syriac letters: tamar.

root.source: Strong’s G5019 Ταρσός: “perhaps the same as (a flat basket)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The city where Paulos was born, "Tarsus of Cilicia, a known city" (Acts 21:39; 22:3); Chananya was told to seek "Sha'ul who is from the city of Tarsus" (Acts 9:10–11). The brothers brought him to Qesarya and sent him to Tarsos (Acts 9:30). Bar-Naba went out to Tarsos to seek Shaul (Acts 11:25).

root.source: Strong’s G5060 Τέρτιος: “of Latin origin” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܛܪܛܝܘܣ. This book prints Tartiyos. The familiar English is Tertius. Read from the Syriac letters: tertios.

root.source: No dictionary source names the origin language (Strong’s G789 Ἄσσος: “probably of foreign origin”); the label follows the Syriac verse form.

names.note: Paulos's companions sailed to the port of Tasus to take him on board there, for he had commanded them so while he went by land (Acts 20:13). They received him from Tasus on the ship and came to Mitylene (Acts 20:14).

The later Syriac text writes this person ܬܘ. This book prints Tau. The familiar English is Omega. Read from the Syriac letters: taw. The same letters are also the ordinary word “come.” Tau is the last letter. Alap, in the same saying, is the first. The familiar pair is Alpha and Omega.

sources.note: The last letter. The Greek pair is Alpha and Omega.

root.source: Strong’s G2291 Θάρα: “of Hebrew origin (H8646)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܬܪܚ. This book prints Terach. The familiar English is Terah. Read from the Syriac letters: tarah.

root.source: Strong’s G5061 Τέρτυλλος: “of uncertain derivation”; Strong’s G5060 Τέρτιος: “of Latin origin” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain). Easton’s Bible Dictionary (1897): “A modification of ‘Tertius’”.

names.note: Chananya the high priest went down with the elders and "with Tertullus the orator," and they informed the governor against Paulos (Acts 24:1). Tertullus began, "In much peace we dwell because of you," and called Paulos "the head of the teaching of the Natsraye" (Acts 24:2, 24:5).

root.source: Strong’s G2332 Θεσσαλονίκη: “from (a Thessalian) and G3529 (νίκη)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Paulos and Shila came to Tesaloniqa, where there was a synagogue of the Yehudaye (Acts 17:1, 17:4), and the Yehudaye of Berua are called more noble than those in Tesaloniqa (Acts 17:10–11). Aristarchus, a Macedonian, was from Tesaloniqa (Acts 20:4; 27:2). The Philippians sent to Paulos's need there once and twice (Philippians 4:15–16), and Demas left Paulos and went to Tesaloniqa (2 Timothy 4:10).

sources.note: The Greek name of the city.

root.source: Strong’s G2331 Θεσσαλονικεύς: “from G2332 (Θεσσαλονίκη)”; Strong’s G2332 Θεσσαλονίκη: “from (a Thessalian) and G3529 (νίκη)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Paulos, Silwanus and Timotheos write "to the assembly of the Thessalonians" in 1 Thessalonians 1:1, and "to the assembly of the Tesaloniquye" in 2 Thessalonians 1:1. Their city is Tesaloniqa, where Paulos spoke in the synagogue for three shabbats (Acts 17:1–2).
The Peshitta writes this person ܬܐܘܦܝܠܐ. This book prints Theophilus. Read from the Syriac letters: Theophilus.

root.source: No dictionary source names the origin language (Strong’s G2363 Θυάτειρα: “of uncertain derivation”); the label follows the Syriac verse form.

names.note: The city of Lydia, the seller of purple who listened to Paulos at Philippi (Acts 16:12, 16:14). Thyatira is one of the seven assemblies to which Revelation is sent, and the Son of Elohim addresses its messenger (Revelation 1:11; 2:18). To the rest in Thyatira who do not hold that teaching, he lays no other burden (Revelation 2:24).

root.source: Strong’s G5085 Τιβεριάς: “from G5086 (Τιβέριος)”; Strong’s G5086 Τιβέριος: “of Latin origin” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain). Easton’s Bible Dictionary (1897): “named by him after the Emperor Tiberius”.

names.note: John 6:1 names the sea of Galila also the sea of Tiberias. After Y'shua fed the crowd, other boats came from Tiberias near the place where they ate the bread (John 6:23). Y'shua showed himself again to his disciples at the sea of Tiberias (John 21:1).

sources.note: The city named for the emperor Tiberius. The Greek writes it this way.

root.source: Strong’s G5086 Τιβέριος: “of Latin origin” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܛܝܒܪܝܘܣ. This book prints Tiberius. Read from the Syriac letters: Tibaryos.

root.source: Strong’s G5090 Τιμαῖος: “probably of Chaldee origin (compare H2931)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܛܝܡܝ. This book prints Timai. The familiar English is Timaeus. Read from the Syriac letters: ṭaymi.

root.source: Strong’s G5096 Τίμων: “from G5092 (τιμή)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܛܝܡܘܢ. This book prints Timon. Read from the Syriac letters: Timon.

root.source: Strong’s G5095 Τιμόθεος: “from G5092 (τιμή) and G2316 (θεός)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: A disciple at Derbe and Lustra, son of a believing Yehudita and an Aramean father, whom Paulos took with him and circumcised (Acts 16:1, 16:3). His faith first dwelt in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5), and Paulos calls him "my true son in the faith" (1 Timothy 1:2). Paulos sent him to strengthen believers in their faith and to remind them of his ways (1 Thessalonians 3:2; 1 Corinthians 4:17).

sources.note: A Greek name, “one who honors God.”

names.note: Paulos's companion, an Aramean who was not compelled to be circumcised when Paulos took him up to Urishlim with Bar-Naba (Galatians 2:1, 2:3). Paulos calls him "a true son in the shared faith" and left him in Crete to appoint elders in every city (Titus 1:4–5). At Corinth, Acts 18:7 names a Titus whose house adjoined the synagogue (Acts 18:1, 18:7); the book does not say they are the same man.

sources.note: A Greek name from the Latin Titus.

root.source: Strong’s G2381 Θωμᾶς: “of Chaldee origin (compare H8380)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: One of the twelve (Matthew 10:3), who is called the Twin (John 20:24; 21:2). He was not with the disciples when Y'shua came, and eight days later Y'shua told him to reach his finger and see his hands (John 20:24, 20:26–27). Toma answered, "My Master and my Elohim!" (John 20:28).

sources.note: Aramaic for twin. The Greek Θωμᾶς is the same word written in Greek letters.

root.source: Strong’s G5139 Τραχωνῖτις: “from a derivative of G5138 (τραχύς)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this place ܛܪܟܘܢܐ. This book prints Trachonitis. Read from the Syriac letters: Trakona.

root.source: Strong’s G5174 Τρωάς: “from (a Trojan)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Paulos and those with him went down from Mysia to the region of Troas, and sailed from Troas to Samothrace (Acts 16:6, 16:8, 16:11). Later they came to Troas from the city of Philipos of Macedonia in five days and stayed there seven days (Acts 20:6). Paulos says a door was opened to him when he came to Troas, and he left a bookcase there with Carpus (2 Corinthians 2:12; 2 Timothy 4:13).

root.source: Strong’s G5161 Τρόφιμος: “from G5160 (τροφή)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Trophimus of Asia was among those who went with Paulos as far as Asia (Acts 20:4). The Yehudaye from Asia had seen "Trophimus the Ephesian" with Paulos in the city and supposed that he had gone into the temple with him (Acts 21:27, 21:29). Paulos writes, "Trophimos I left while sick in the city of Militos" (2 Timothy 4:20).

root.source: Strong’s G4558 Σάρεπτα: “of Hebrew origin (H6886)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this place ܨܪܦܬ. This book prints Tsarfat. The familiar English is Zarephath. Read from the Syriac letters: Tsarfat.

root.source: Strong’s G4605 Σιδών: “of Hebrew origin (H6721)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Y'shua went to the borders of Tsur and Tsidon (Matthew 15:21; Mark 7:24), and people from there came to him (Mark 3:8; Luke 6:17). He said it would be more comfortable for Tsur and Tsidon in the day of judgment than for Korazin and Beth-Tsayda (Matthew 11:21–22). On Paulos's voyage the ship reached Tsidon, where the centurion let him go to his friends (Acts 27:3).

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Sidon. The Greek is Σιδών.

root.source: Strong’s G4622 Σιών: “of Hebrew origin (H6726)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: When Y'shua rode a donkey's colt into Urishlim, Matthew gives the prophet's words "Say to the daughter of Tsehyon, Look, your king comes to you" (Matthew 21:4–5, 21:7), and John gives "Do not fear, daughter of Tsiyon. Look, your king comes to you" (John 12:12, 12:14–15). Paulos and Keefa quote the writing about a stone laid in Tsiyon: whoever believes in him will not be ashamed (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6). Hebrews 12:22 speaks of the mountain of Tsiyon and the Urishlim that is in heaven, and in Revelation 14:1 the Lamb stands on the mountain of Tsiyon.

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Zion. The Greek is Σιών.

root.source: Strong’s G5184 Τύρος: “of Hebrew origin (H6865): Tyrus (i.e. Tsor), a place in Palestine” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: Y'shua went to the borders of Tsur and Tsidon (Matthew 15:21; Mark 7:24), and said it would be more comfortable for Tsur and Tsidon in the day of judgment than for Korazin and Beth-Tsayda (Matthew 11:21–22). On Paulos's voyage the ship unloaded its cargo at Tsur, and from there they sailed to Akko (Acts 21:3, 21:7).

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Tyre. The Greek is Τύρος.

root.source: Strong’s G5190 Τυχικός: “from a derivative of G5177 (τυγχάνω)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: One of those from Asia who went out with Paulos, with Trophimus (Acts 20:4). Paulos calls him "a beloved brother and faithful minister in our Master" and sends him to make his news known (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7). He writes, "Tukikos I have sent to Ephesos" (2 Timothy 4:12), and tells Titus that he will send Artima or Tukikos to him (Titus 3:12).

root.source: Strong’s G5181 Τύραννος: “a provincial form of the derivative of the base of G2962 (κύριος)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: When some at Ephesos hardened themselves and reviled the way of Elohim, Paulos separated the disciples and spoke with them every day in the school of a man named Tyrannus (Acts 19:1, 19:9). This continued two years, until all who dwell in Asia heard the word of Master YHWH (Acts 19:10).

root.source: Strong’s G2414 Ἱεροσόλυμα: “of Hebrew origin (H3389)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The city where Y'shua's people went every year at the feast of the Passover (Luke 2:41), and where he said he must go to suffer, be killed and rise on the third day (Matthew 16:21). The proclaiming in his name was to begin from Urishlim (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8), and the apostles and elders were there when Paulos and Bar-Naba went up about the dispute (Acts 15:2). Revelation 21:2 sees the holy city, new Urishlim, coming down out of heaven from Elohim.

sources.note: The Hebrew writing of Jerusalem. The Greek uses Ἱεροσόλυμα and Ἰερουσαλήμ.

root.source: Strong’s G3774 Οὐρίας: “of Hebrew origin (H223)” (Strong’s Greek Dictionary, 1890, public domain).

names.note: The Peshitta writes this person ܐܘܪܝܐ. This book prints Uriya. The familiar English is Uriah. Read from the Syriac letters: urya. The same letters are also the ordinary word “the stall.”
